title: Best Commercial Dehumidifier (2026): LGR Units for Job Sites
h1: The Best Commercial Dehumidifiers for Restoration and Job Sites
dek: When a building is wet, not just humid, you need a machine that drains itself, shrugs off the cold and keeps pulling water long after a home unit gives up.
description: The best commercial dehumidifiers for flood restoration, job sites and crawl spaces: heavy-duty LGR units compared on AHAM pints, coverage and pump lift.
intro: A burst pipe, a flooded basement or a new build full of fresh concrete puts more water into the air than any household dehumidifier was designed to handle. Consumer 50-pint units are built to keep a room comfortable over a summer. A **commercial dehumidifier** is built to dry a structure — fast, unattended and often in a cold, dusty space — before mold gets a foothold.

Almost every serious machine in this class uses **LGR (Low Grain Refrigerant)** technology, carries a built-in condensate pump and lives in a rugged housing with wheels. The real differences come down to how much water each one pulls under realistic conditions, how much floor area it can handle and how much you want to pay for brand reputation and service networks.
We sorted six restoration-grade units by the job they suit best, and we compare them on the AHAM rating rather than the much bigger saturation number printed on the box.
topPicksLead: For most contractors and homeowners facing a real water problem, the **AlorAir Storm LGR Extreme** is the one to buy: restoration-grade LGR drying, a self-draining pump and a five-year warranty at a fraction of legacy-brand cost.

blocks.text: We don't run a test lab or a restoration crew, so we lean on the numbers that can be compared across brands: AHAM-condition pint ratings, coverage claims, pump lift, minimum operating temperature and warranty terms from manufacturer spec sheets and manuals. We check the CPSC recall database for every brand we consider.

Then we read what professionals and owners say after months of use — pump failures, defrost problems, how easily parts can be found. We weighted LGR performance and self-draining highest, because those are the features that separate a real restoration tool from an oversized household box.

sections.heading: What to look for in a commercial-grade dehumidifier

items.label: Compare AHAM pints, not saturation
items.text: The giant number on the box is measured at 90°F and 90% humidity — a freshly flooded basement for a few hours. The AHAM rating (80°F, 60%) is closer to what you'll see across a real job.

items.label: LGR or SLGR for restoration
items.text: Standard refrigerant units lose steam once the air is moderately dry. LGR designs pre-cool incoming air so they keep condensing water, which is what finishes off wet framing and subfloor.

items.label: A built-in condensate pump
items.text: On a job site nobody is around to empty a bucket. A pump that lifts water to a window, sink or drain lets the unit run for days.

items.label: Cold-weather defrost
items.text: Crawl spaces and unheated basements can sit in the 40s. Without auto-defrost, a coil ices over and the machine stops removing water. Our [guide to a freezing dehumidifier](/guides/dehumidifier-freezing-up/) explains why.

items.label: Capacity matched to the water load
items.text: One wet room, a crawl space or a garage suits an 85-pint AHAM unit. A whole floor or a warehouse calls for 125–140 pints — or several smaller machines spread across the wettest areas.

blocks.text: A conventional dehumidifier pulls air across a cold coil and collects whatever condenses. As the room dries, there's less water to condense and output drops off sharply. An LGR unit routes incoming air past the cold outgoing air first, pre-cooling it so it reaches its dew point sooner on the main coil. The result is a machine that keeps extracting water at humidity levels where a household unit has effectively quit.

That's why restoration standards lean on LGR equipment, and why these machines are the right call for a [water-damage dry-out](/best/best-dehumidifier-for-water-damage/) but the wrong one for keeping a finished basement at 50%. For ongoing comfort, a 50-pint household unit is cheaper, quieter and plenty.

blocks.title: Commercial vs. residential in one line
blocks.text: Residential units are rated for 20–50 pints a day and built for seasonal comfort. Commercial LGR units pull roughly 75–140+ pints a day at AHAM, drain themselves, survive job sites and run near freezing.

For a single flood, renting for a few days often costs less than buying. The math changes if you own rental properties, live where pipes freeze, have a chronically wet crawl space or have filed a water claim before. In those cases a machine you already own can be running within an hour instead of a day, and a commercial unit typically pays for itself after one or two incidents.

items: **Rent** for a one-time event, especially if your insurer is covering mitigation.
**Buy** if you'll use it more than once, need it immediately when water hits or run a trade business.
**Install a ducted system** if the space needs humidity control year-round rather than emergency drying.

faqs.q: What is the best commercial dehumidifier?
faqs.a: For most contractors and homeowners with a serious water problem, the AlorAir Storm LGR Extreme. It's rated at 85 pints a day at AHAM (180 at saturation), covers up to about 2,300 sq ft, drains itself through a built-in pump with 14.7 ft of lift and carries a five-year warranty.

faqs.q: What does LGR mean on a dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Low Grain Refrigerant. An LGR unit pre-cools incoming air before it reaches the main coil, so it can keep condensing moisture even when the air is already fairly dry — down to around 40 grains of water per pound of air. That's what makes it the standard for drying out framing and subfloors after water damage.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a heavy-duty commercial dehumidifier and a home unit?
faqs.a: Home units are rated at roughly 20–50 pints a day and are built for seasonal comfort. Commercial units pull far more water, use LGR technology to reach lower humidity, have built-in pumps, rugged housings and wheels, and keep running in cold spaces near freezing.

faqs.q: How big a commercial dehumidifier do I need?
faqs.a: Size it to the water load as well as the floor area. A single flooded room, garage or crawl space is well served by an 85-pint AHAM unit. A whole floor, warehouse or large new build needs 125–140 pints at AHAM, or several smaller machines placed where it's wettest.

faqs.q: Can I use a commercial dehumidifier in a basement?
faqs.a: Yes, and many people do after a flood or for a chronically wet basement or crawl space. For routine dampness, though, a household 50-pint unit is cheaper to buy and run and much quieter. A commercial machine earns its keep when you need to dry building materials fast, before mold sets in.

faqs.q: Do commercial dehumidifiers need a floor drain?
faqs.a: No. The units on this list have built-in condensate pumps that push water up and out through a hose to a window, sink or drain. You can also gravity-drain them when the unit sits above the drain point.

faqs.q: Can you rent a commercial dehumidifier?
faqs.a: Yes. Equipment-rental counters and restoration suppliers rent LGR units by the day or week, and renting is usually the cheaper route for a single flood. If you expect to need one more than once, owning means it's running the moment water hits. Our [dehumidifier rental guide](/guides/dehumidifier-rental/) covers typical day rates.
